title: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent”. Scope: fossil and living species of all groups

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-24: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing fossil and morphological matrices allow direct tests in many groups. Coverage is far from all groups, and convergence can mimic morphological intermediacy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place fossil taxa in morphological character space and phylogenies with extant groups, then quantify whether fossils disproportionately occupy positions between living clades. Excess intermediate placement relative to null and preservation-aware expectations supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Morphological matrices are concentrated in well-studied clades.

Intermediate character states depend on character selection and tree model.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Morphospace position between living groups is a concrete variable, and many published matrices already combine fossil and living taxa. Those matrices cover vertebrates and shelly invertebrates far better than the full tree of life, so the scope is partial. The analysis is standard but slow to harmonize, and character choice can nudge fossils toward intermediate scores.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place fossil species in morphospace and on trees with living members of the same groups, and ask whether fossils occupy positions between living subgroups more often than a random-extinction null. An excess of intermediate placements would confirm the claim; fossils nested inside living subgroups as often as that null would refute a general intermediate-stem pattern.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Soft-bodied and poorly fossilized groups are almost absent.

Character matrices are clade-specific and unevenly published.

Stem-group fossils are expected to look intermediate under the hypothesis being tested, which can shade into circular coding.
